queries.diagnose: When your worth depends on their praise, every word of blame shakes you; craving approval keeps the mind unsteady and the heart restless.
queries.steady: Praise and blame come and go, but your own truth is what you must hold; the life you build with your own hands is real regardless of their question.
queries.act: Let go of seeking their approval on this one thing, and turn your attention to what you can control today, one shift at a time.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः ॥
verse.line: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.
verse.translation: Better is one's own duty, even done imperfectly, than the duty of another well done. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is full of fear.
verse.why: Your own path, imperfectly walked, beats a borrowed one.
verse.misuse: Not 'stay in the role your family or birth assigned you'. It's about being true to your own nature and calling.

prasang.title: The ignorant and the wise; act free of like and dislike
prasang.summary: Krishna contrasts the attached and the wise, warns that ego claims credit for what nature does, and says to follow your own path rather than imitate another's.
prasang.lesson: Your own path, imperfectly walked, beats a borrowed one.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield, where Arjuna is frozen by doubt and grief. Krishna sees the danger in Arjuna trying to copy someone else's duty instead of his own. The verse says that your own path, even if you stumble on it, is far safer and better than living someone else's life perfectly. Borrowed lives carry a hidden fear because they are not yours. It is a call to act from your own nature rather than imitating another.
verse.for_you: You are sending your money home and working the night shifts. That is your path, and it is heavy. Your own duty done imperfectly is better than a borrowed life done perfectly.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: Opening verse of 'Advice to the Mind'.
verse.sanskrit: परेषां चेतांसि प्रतिदिवसमाराध्य बहुधा प्रसादं किं नेतुं विशसि हृदय क्लेशकलितम् । प्रसन्ने त्वय्यन्तः स्वयमुदितचिन्तामणिगणो विविक्तः संकल्पः किमभिलषितं पुष्यति न ते ॥
verse.line: Why exhaust yourself daily winning others' approval? Settle inside, and your own clarity grants every wish.
verse.translation: O heart, why do you enter into weariness, day after day trying to please the minds of others in so many ways, to win their favour? When you are at peace within, your own clear resolve rises by itself like a cluster of wish-granting gems: what wish of yours would it not fulfil?
verse.why: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Advice to the mind
prasang.summary: The poet talks to his own mind: why exhaust yourself pleasing others, why replay the past and script the future, why roam everywhere but within. 'So what?' asks what all our gains amount to.
prasang.lesson: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to his own heart. He asks why it wears itself out trying to win the favor of others every single day. He says that when you settle inside yourself, your own clear resolve rises by itself like a cluster of wish-granting gems. Then he asks what wish of yours would that not fulfill.
verse.for_you: That half-salary you send home is real care. But the restless test you rehearse on every call is one you invented. Your own settled mind is the only approval that will let your thoughts rest.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु गच्छतु वा यथेष्टम् । अद्यैव वा मरणमस्तु युगान्तरे वा न्याय्यात्पथः प्रविचलन्ति पदं न धीराः ॥
verse.line: Let them praise or blame, let money come or go: the steady don't step off the right path.
verse.translation: Let the worldly-wise blame or praise; let fortune come or go as she pleases; let death come today or ages hence: the steadfast do not move a step from the path of what is right.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to you from the page, not from a throne. They have seen the world praise one person and blame another, watched money arrive and vanish, and looked at the coming and going of life. They say the steady do not move a step from the path of what is right. This means the people around you may change their minds, the money you send may feel heavy or light, but your own truth remains. It does not shift because someone asks a different question. The path you walk is yours alone.
verse.for_you: You send half your salary home and hold your parents' pride. Their next question about marriage will come, but it does not move you off your path. You keep walking the life you chose.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, describing the qualities of the person dear to God.
verse.sanskrit: तुल्यनिन्दास्तुतिर्मौनी सन्तुष्टो येनकेनचित् । अनिकेतः स्थिरमतिर्भक्तिमान्मे प्रियो नरः ॥
verse.line: Praise and blame weigh the same. Quiet, content with what comes, rooted in steadiness, not status.
verse.translation: to whom blame and praise are equal, who is silent, content with whatever comes, without a fixed home, steady in mind and full of devotion, that person is dear to me.
verse.why: Kindness without hatred, steadiness in praise and blame: that's what's loved.
verse.misuse: Not 'never ask for credit'. You can advocate for yourself without letting praise or blame define you.

prasang.title: The marks of one dear to God
prasang.summary: Krishna lists the marks of one dear to him: no hatred, friendly and compassionate, forgiving, content, disturbing no one and disturbed by no one, the same in praise and blame.
prasang.lesson: Kindness without hatred, steadiness in praise and blame: that's what's loved.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield, listing the marks of a person who is dear to God. He says that to this person, blame and praise weigh the same. They are quiet and content with whatever comes. They are steady in mind, rooted in devotion, and do not cling to status or a fixed home. The verse proposes that kindness without hatred and steadiness in praise and blame is what is truly loved.
verse.for_you: You send half your salary home and your parents praise you for it. Yet the same voice asks when you will marry, and the shame feels heavier than the praise ever lifts. This verse says that the steadiness you are looking for is not in their approval, but in your own mind.

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: Vasishtha tells Rama how to steer his own habits.
verse.sanskrit: समता सांत्वनेनाशु न द्रागिति शनेशनेः । पौरुषेणैव यत्नेन पालयेच्चित्तबालकम् ॥
verse.line: Raise your mind like a child: gently, patiently, little by little, never by force.
verse.translation: With evenness and gentle coaxing, not in a rush but little by little, by steady effort, look after the child that is your mind.
verse.why: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

prasang.title: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha is speaking to Rama about steering his own habits. He says to raise your mind like a child: gently, patiently, little by little, never by force. Your past effort shaped today. Today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands. Look after the child that is your mind with evenness and gentle coaxing, not in a rush.
verse.for_you: The marriage talk is a habit that formed long before you could choose it. You do not need to force your mind into stillness right now. Just notice the restlessness without fighting it, and let your own effort, not their approval, shape what comes next.

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: Vasishtha on effort and grace, after Prahlada's story.
verse.sanskrit: नित्याभ्यासविवेकाभ्यां चित्तमाशु प्रसीदति । आम्र एव दशामेति साहकारीं शनैः शनैः ॥
verse.line: Daily practice and clear thinking make the mind clear, slowly, the way a mango ripens.
verse.translation: Through daily practice and discernment the mind soon becomes clear, just as a mango slowly ripens into its sweetness.
verse.why: Grace and effort work together; keep practising daily, and let the mind ripen slowly.

prasang.title: Prahlada: effort and grace are not rivals
prasang.summary: After telling how Prahlada awakened, Vasishtha faces Rama's challenge: if everything comes by effort, wasn't Prahlada saved by Vishnu's grace? Vasishtha answers that Prahlada earned it himself, that the Self and Vishnu are not two, and that sometimes we wake by our own effort and sometimes by grace reached through devotion. Steady daily practice ripens the mind like a mango.
prasang.lesson: Grace and effort work together; keep practising daily, and let the mind ripen slowly.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha speaks to Rama after the story of Prahlada. He tells Rama that waking up is not only about Vishnu's grace. Prahlada earned his awakening through his own steady effort. The Self and Vishnu are one. A mind becomes clear and sweet through daily practice and discernment. It ripens slowly, just like a mango. You do your part, and let the rest unfold in its own time.
verse.for_you: The call with your parents will ask about marriage again. You cannot control their questions today. You can only do your one small part. Keep your mind on your shift, on the road home, on your own steady practice. Let the rest ripen slowly.

story.title: Satyakama Jabala, the honest boy
story.story_hook: Satyakama wanted to study, but first he had to ask his mother a question she could not answer.
story.summary: A boy who wants to study asks his mother about his father's lineage. She tells him frankly she does not know, and he repeats this word for word to the teacher. The teacher accepts him for his honesty, sends him off with 400 weak cows, and the boy returns years later with a thousand, having learned from nature along the way, yet still asks his teacher to teach him.
story.lesson: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.

anchor.speaker: Jabala
anchor.setting: A boy asks his mother his lineage before seeking a teacher.
anchor.sanskrit: सा हैनमुवाच नाहमेतद्वेद तात यद्गोत्रस्त्वमसि बह्वहं चरन्ती परिचारिणी यौवने त्वामलभे साहमेतन्न वेद यद्गोत्रस्त्वमसि जबाला तु नामाहमस्मि सत्यकामो नाम त्वमसि स सत्यकाम एव जाबालो ब्रवीथा इति ॥
anchor.line: His mother said, 'I don't know your father's line. I am Jabala, you are Satyakama. Say exactly that.'
anchor.translation: She said to him: 'I do not know your lineage, my child. In my youth I moved about a great deal as a serving woman, and then I had you. So I do not know your lineage. My name is Jabala and your name is Satyakama. Just say you are Satyakama Jabala.'
anchor.why: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.

story.hook_title: A boy didn't know who his father was, and told his teacher the truth anyway
story.teaser: A boy didn't know who his father was, and told his teacher the truth anyway
story.for_you: Satyakama did not hide his uncertain beginnings. He simply told the truth and went to learn. You do not need to have your whole life mapped out to be worthy of your parents' pride or your own respect.

script: You are carrying pride and shame at the same time. Your parents are proud of you, but every call ends with the same question. You are working long night shifts, sending half your salary home, and you feel like you are failing a test you never agreed to take.
Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way. Krishna said to Arjuna:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात्, स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः.
In plain words: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.

Krishna is telling Arjuna that it is better to walk your own path, even if you stumble on it. A borrowed life, even if it looks perfect to everyone else, is full of fear because it is not yours. The danger is not the mistakes you make on your own road. The danger is trying to live someone else's life. This is easier said than done, because you are trying to prove your worth to your parents. You are measuring your own heavy path against a life that looks easier from a distance.

You are working the night shifts and sending your money home. That is your path, and it is heavy. Your own duty done imperfectly is better than a borrowed life done perfectly. You do not have to answer the question about marriage today. You only have to keep walking your own road, even when it feels uneven.
What is your own path asking you to do today?

depth.life: You are sending your salary home and working the night shifts. That is your own path, heavy and real. Yet your mind keeps running to the marriage question, as if you are failing a test they set up.
depth.points: The approval you seek from them is not the one that will settle your mind. The test you are failing is the one you built for yourself, not the one they are asking about.
depth.practice: Name one small choice today that is only yours. Let it be imperfect. Do not try to earn their pride with it.
depth.question: What would your own duty look like if you stopped trying to pass their test?
